The attached patch makes NFS share superblocks between mounts from the same
server and FSID over the same protocol.
It does this by creating each superblock with a false root and returning the
real root dentry in the vfsmount presented by get_sb(). The root dentry set
starts off as an anonymous dentry if we don't already have the dentry for its
inode
column2: otherwise it simply returns the dentry we already have.

column1: We may thus end up with several trees of dentries in the superblock
column2: and if at

column1: some later point one of anonymous tree roots is discovered by normal filesystem
activity to be located in another tree within the superblock
column2: the anonymous

column1: root is named and materialises attached to the second tree at the appropriate
point.
Why do it this way? Why not pass an extra argument to the mount() syscall to
indicate the subpath and then pathwalk from the server root to the desired
directory? You can't guarantee this will work for two reasons:
(1) The root and intervening nodes may not be accessible to the client.
With NFS2 and NFS3
column2: for instance
column3: mountd is called on the server to get

column1: the filehandle for the tip of a path. mountd won't give us handles for
anything we don't have permission to access
column2: and so we can't set up NFS

column1: inodes for such nodes
column2: and so can't easily set up dentries (we'd have to

column1: have ghost inodes or something).
With this patch we don't actually create dentries until we get handles
from the server that we can use to set up their inodes
column2: and we don't

column1: actually bind them into the tree until we know for sure where they go.
(2) Inaccessible symbolic links.
If we're asked to mount two exports from the server
column2: eg:

column1: mount warthog:/warthog/aaa/xxx /mmm
mount warthog:/warthog/bbb/yyy /nnn
We may not be able to access anything nearer the root than xxx and yyy
but we may find out later that /mmm/www/yyy
column2: say

column1: directory as the one mounted on /nnn. What we might then find out
column2: for

column1: example
column2: is that /warthog/bbb was actually a symbolic link to

column1: /warthog/aaa/xxx/www
column2: but we can't actually determine that by talking to

column1: the server until /warthog is made available by NFS.
This would lead to having constructed an errneous dentry tree which we
can't easily fix. We can end up with a dentry marked as a directory when
it should actually be a symlink
column2: or we could end up with an apparently

column1: hardlinked directory.
With this patch we need not make assumptions about the type of a dentry
for which we can't retrieve information
column2: nor need we assume we know its

column1: place in the grand scheme of things until we actually see that place.
This patch reduces the possibility of aliasing in the inode and page caches for
inodes that may be accessed by more than one NFS export. It also reduces the
number of superblocks required for NFS where there are many NFS exports being
used from a server (home directory server + autofs for example).
This in turn makes it simpler to do local caching of network filesystems
column2: as it

column1: can then be guaranteed that there won't be links from multiple inodes in
separate superblocks to the same cache file.
Obviously
column2: cache aliasing between different levels of NFS protocol could still

column1: be a problem
column2: but at least that gives us another key to use when indexing the

column1: cache.
This patch makes the following changes:
(1) The server record construction/destruction has been abstracted out into
its own set of functions to make things easier to get right.  These have
been moved into fs/nfs/client.c.
All the code in fs/nfs/client.c has to do with the management of
connections to servers
column2: and doesn't touch superblocks in any way; the

column1: remaining code in fs/nfs/super.c has to do with VFS superblock management.
(2) The sequence of events undertaken by NFS mount is now reordered:
(a) A volume representation (struct nfs_server) is allocated.
(b) A server representation (struct nfs_client) is acquired.  This may be
allocated or shared
column2: and is keyed on server address

column1: version.
(c) If allocated
column2: the client representation is initialised.  The state

column1: member variable of nfs_client is used to prevent a race during
initialisation from two mounts.
(d) For NFS4 a simple pathwalk is performed
column2: walking from FH to FH to find

column1: the root filehandle for the mount (fs/nfs/getroot.c).  For NFS2/3 we
are given the root FH in advance.
(e) The volume FSID is probed for on the root FH.
(f) The volume representation is initialised from the FSINFO record
retrieved on the root FH.
(g) sget() is called to acquire a superblock.  This may be allocated or
shared
column2: keyed on client pointer and FSID.

column1: (h) If allocated
column2: the superblock is initialised.

column1: (i) If the superblock is shared
column2: then the new nfs_server record is

column1: discarded.
(j) The root dentry for this mount is looked up from the root FH.
(k) The root dentry for this mount is assigned to the vfsmount.
(3) nfs_readdir_lookup() creates dentries for each of the entries readdir()
returns; this function now attaches disconnected trees from alternate
roots that happen to be discovered attached to a directory being read (in
the same way nfs_lookup() is made to do for lookup ops).
The new d_materialise_unique() function is now used to do this
column2: thus

column1: permitting the whole thing to be done under one set of locks
column2: and thus

column1: avoiding any race between mount and lookup operations on the same
directory.
(4) The client management code uses a new debug facility: NFSDBG_CLIENT which
is set by echoing 1024 to /proc/net/sunrpc/nfs_debug.
(5) Clone mounts are now called xdev mounts.
(6) Use the dentry passed to the statfs() op as the handle for retrieving fs
statistics rather than the root dentry of the superblock (which is now a
dummy).
